newsitem.title: UK: Crunchtime looms as DTB takes on LIFFE over Bunds.
newsitem.headline: Crunchtime looms as DTB takes on LIFFE over Bunds.

text.p: The dog days of August typically mark a slack trading period, but for two rival futures exchanges this month is a potential turning point in a long-running battle.
Frankfurt's DTB and London's LIFFE, both of which list German Bund futures, are fighting for market share in the runup to a single European currency.
LIFFE, which operates on an "open outcry" basis with traders dealing face to face, has been the dominant player, but there are signs the DTB's electronic technology is gaining favour.
In July, the DTB said it traded 43 percent of the total market in Bund futures, its largest share to date.
"We are improving, and our trading volume will be more than on LIFFE," said Dirk Aufderheide, DTB broker at Deutsche Bank in Frankfurt.
The DTB turned up the heat when it extended its trading hours on August 1 to a 1700 GMT finish, in line with LIFFE.
"We did it in response to demand from members, who wanted the same opening hours as LIFFE," said a DTB official.
Success in the Bund future is crucial, because Bund futures on LIFFE and the DTB will vie with Paris-listed French government bond futures for benchmark euro bond status.

LIFFE has this year overtaken the Chicago Mercantile Exchange as the world's second largest futures exchange. LIFFE almost matched its record month for volume in July, yet the Bund future, once its flagship contract, declined in turnover.
The DTB operates seamlessly via its electronic system during a session, while LIFFE traders must move from pit to screens when the floor shuts, with minutes of down-time in between.
The DTB's electronic system is a major factor in its recent success, dealers said. Also, liquidity is improving and costs for brokers can be lower since they need not run a pit booth.

"You have the transparency, the ability to see bids and offers above and below the current price," said one trader from a German bank in London. "The arbitrageurs love that -- because of it, they can trade."

Critics say the DTB contract could not survive alone, but feeds off arbitrage between the two exchanges. The exchanges say arbitrage only accounts for around 10 percent of Bund trade, but unofficial estimates put arbitrage as high as 60 percent.
But the growth of terminals outside Germany is allowing the DTB to reach a base beyond the arbitrageurs, participants said.
Of the 168 DTB members, there are 71 with terminals outside Germany, according to the DTB. Volume generated by seven members in the U.S. alone accounts for nine percent of turnover.
The system's scope for "direct entry" appeals to clients, dealers said. "Hedge funds can gain access to the DTB without going through any broker," said Aufderheide.
The DTB is looking to make the trading of its contracts more global, with an agreement with Singapore exchange SIMEX to trade Bund and shorter-dated Bobl contracts by March 1998.
The agreement provides competition for LIFFE's existing trading link with the Chicago Board of Trade, which encompasses Bund contracts.
Meanwhile, LIFFE is fighting to keep supremacy, with the September listing of Bobl contracts, of which it previously tried and failed to make a success.
LIFFE is bullish on prospects for the Bobl this time around, after delisting Bobl futures in the early 1990s.

"There has been a change in the underlying cash market, with a greater proportion traded in London, and the Bobl has become a much more attractive instrument," said Karin Forseke, chief operating officer of LIFFE.
LIFFE's strong options business increases its market share for Bund derivatives as a whole, and should help it make inroads into the DTB's Bobl option, dealers said.
Bobl contracts also help LIFFE counter the argument that only DTB members have the ability to trade the entire German yield curve.
LIFFE's open-outcry system also has its attractions.

"The DTB cannot cope so well with a fast market. For U.S. employment data, the business reverts to LIFFE," the London trader said. "The DTB may trade the some volume as LIFFE, but overtake it? Never."
